hints: Start by reminding yourself what an ideal gas assumes, that particles have no attractions for each other and take up no space.
Think about what pushes real molecules close together and slows them down, so attractions start to matter.
Now ask which change makes real molecules ignore each other more, matching the ideal assumption.
walkthrough:
**Recall the ideal gas model**

An ideal gas is a perfect model where we pretend two things are true. There are zero intermolecular forces, and the particles themselves have negligible volume.

Ideal assumptions:
$$\text{no attractions between particles, negligible particle volume}$$

**See when real gases break the model**

Real gases deviate when molecules get close together or move slowly. High pressure squeezes them together, and low temperature lowers kinetic energy so attractions can take hold.

So ideal behaviour needs the opposite: low pressure and high temperature.

**Apply this to molecular properties**

Polar molecules have stronger dipole-dipole attractions, so they deviate more. Non-polar molecules with very weak London forces, like $\text{He}$ and $\text{H}_2$, are closest to having zero attraction.

Therefore weaker intermolecular forces make ideal behaviour more likely.

options.A: Higher pressure squeezes molecules very close together. The volume of the particles is no longer negligible and attractions become significant, so deviation from ideal increases, not decreases.
options.B: Lower temperature means less kinetic energy. Molecules move slowly enough for intermolecular forces to pull them together, leading toward liquefaction and large deviation from $pV = nRT$.
options.C: More polar molecules have stronger permanent dipole-dipole forces. This is the opposite of the ideal assumption of zero attraction, so deviation increases.
options.D: Weaker intermolecular forces means the gas is closer to the key ideal assumption of no attractions between particles. This is why small, non-polar gases approach ideal behaviour best.
